title.narrative: Output 6.3. Increased capacity of member States to develop gender-responsive legislation, policies and measures for a world of work free from violence and harassment

description.narrative:
From January to May 2020, the Commission for Employment Equity (CEE) together with the National Department of Employment and Labour reviewed the Code of Good Practice on the handling of sexual harassment cases in the workplace to assess its alignment with the provisions of C190. To address the identified gaps, the CEE and the National Department of Employment and Labour instituted a process for the adoption of a new Code of Good Practice on the Elimination and Prevention of Harassment in the workplace in line with C190. The draft Code that is now tabled for negotiations at the National Economic and Development Council (NEDLAC) is intended to address the prevention, elimination and management of harassment at work. The draft Code will be finalized and submitted for adoption to Cabinet by end November 2021.
The Business Unity South Africa (BUSA), a representative employers' organization, took measures to increase the capacity of its members on issues related to violence and harassment. In particular, in August 2021 BUSA instituted a pilot intervention to promote workplace programmes to handle violence and harassment in the workplace. To this end, BUSA has undertaken an audit of practical experiences enterprise level at the national and sectoral level to consolidate good practices violence and harassment in the workplace. This information is aimed at sharing good practices and at producing a fact sheet on handling violence and harassment in the workplace for broader dissemination to affiliate members. With contributions from RBSA, the ILO from October 2020 to February 2021 facilitated capacity support for the drafting of the Code and facilitated technical inputs and comments on the draft, which was tabled at the National Economic Development and Labour Council (NEDLAC) in March 2021.
With contributions drawn from RBSA, the ILO provided support to BUSA. In particular, the ILO facilitated and coordinated a capacity building workshop for 6 affiliate members of BUSA in May 2021 to raise their awareness on provisions of C190 and its accompanying Recommendation 206.
In September 2021, the ILO collaborated with BUSA to facilitate a follow up capacity building workshop for affiliate members on C190, and on the draft Code of Good Practice on Eliminating Harassment in the Workplace. The ILO also supported BUSA in its efforts towards increased awareness of its members on available facilities to which employers can refer their workers to seek psycho-therapy services in the event of violence and harassment. In this regard, the ILO has also provided technical assistance in the development of a BUSA register of facilities that can be used by employers in case of employees seeking services if affected by violence and harassment in the workplace.

description.narrative: Government and the Social Partners represented in a National Tripartite-Plus task team facilitating the transition of the informal economy to formal economy, commissioned an in-depth gender sensitive diagnostic on barriers to formalization in December 2020. The study undertook an analytical review of policies, laws, regulations and support programmes and initiatives that have an impact on the registration, formalization and development of informal economic units as enterprises and their compliance with labour laws, and to identify constraints and barriers, including on account of gender inequality and discrimination, to formalisation. The diagnostic study also sought to identify strategic gender support needs of both women and men informal economy workers and units in the context of COVID-19 with respect to formalisation. In a national validation workshop held virtually in March 2021, Government and the Social Partners validated the findings of the study and reached consensus to draw from the study to make policy proposals. By July 2021, Women in Informal Employment: Globalizing and Organizing (WIEGO), a global network established a database of women Home Based Workers drawn from the informal economy. A total of 40 home based workers from across four provinces in South Africa have been registered in the database. The database is managed by WIEGO to facilitate support services to the home based workers, including procurement opportunities offered by public sector institutions and access to Government relief schemes and programmes instituted by Government to mitigate the health and socioeconomic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on enterprises and workers in the informal economy. In September 2020, the ILO facilitated discussion by a tripartite-plus ad-hoc working group for the design of terms of reference for a gender responsive diagnostic study on barriers to formalization. Members of the tripartite-plus ad-hoc working group were drawn from a national task team that has been in existence for several years to facilitate the transition of the informal economy to formal economy. With contributions from RBSA the ILO in December 2020 commissioned the diagnostic study on barriers to formalization. ILO also facilitated engagement by the research team with Government partners and the Social Partners in a series of in-depth interviews. The ILO also hosted and coordinated a tripartite-plus validation workshop in May 2020 where the findings of the research were presented and discussed. ILO has begun a process to publish the research report for broad dissemination. With contributions from RBSA, the ILO partnered with WIEGO in December 2020 for the establishment of a national database of women owned homebased worker organizations and individual home-based workers to facilitate a transparent and centralized mechanism for the procurement of products from home based workers to meet current and future demands by public sector institutions. The ILO co-created this intervention in with WIEGO by defining the terms of reference for the establishment of the database. The ILO also provided technical inputs and advisory support in the conceptualization of a temporary in-house Call Centre that was used to reach out to home based workers for purposes of registering them on the database. ILO advisory was also provided in the design of a media campaign launched to reach out to home based workers to encourage them to register on the database, and in the analysis of the data collected. To-date, this intervention has culminated in the registration of 40 women owned home based workers and organizations.

Output 7.2. Increased capacity of member States to ensure safe and healthy working conditions

description.narrative:
In April 2020, the Government of South Africa in consultation with the Social Partners in the National Economic and Development Council (NEDLAC) developed and gazetted COVID-19 OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY MEASURES IN WORKPLACES (C19 OHS) Direction in terms of regulation 10 (8) of the Disaster Management Act. According to Labour Inspectors' reports submitted in 2020 to the Chief Inspector of the National Department of Employment and Labour, the overall workplace compliance rate with the Directions was 56%. Subsequent Directives gazetted in 2020 by the National Department of Employment and Labour built on April Regulations.
The National Department of Employment and Labour in collaboration with the Social Partners and membership based organizations in the informal economy, developed and adopted Occupational health and safety guidelines (OSH) guidelines and a COVID-19 Communication Strategy for informal economy, targeting in particular waste pickers, street vendors and home based workers. The OSH Guidelines and COVID-19 Communication were validated in June 2021 by Government and the Social Partners and were submitted in August 2021 for adoption by the Senior Management of the National Department of Employment and Labour. The OSH Guidelines and COVID-19 Communication Strategy were formally adopted by National Department of Employment and Labour and it was operationalized at the end of 2021. In April 2020 the ILO co-hosted the virtual commemoration of World Day for Safety and Health in Africa in collaboration with African Union Development Agency (AUDA-NEPAD) AUDA-NEPAD and other partners. In May 2020, the ILO collaborated with the AUDA-NEPAD to host and facilitate a series of on-line courses on various topics relating to the management of COVID-19 and OSH for an estimated 600 South African based individuals including employers and workers' representatives, OSH Inspectorate officials from Labour, Health and Mines, local authority officials, OSH professionals. The online course covered topics including the following; Setting up COVID-19 coordination team and work streams, Epidemiology and management of COVID-19 in the workplace, Return to work post COVID-19 illness & lock-down, Implications of COVID-19 in the workplace, as well as COVID-19 Health Risk Assessment and workplace control measures. The trainings on OSH and COVID-19 have enabled the National Department of Employment and Labour (DEL) to be able to technically support inspectors in the field. The Inspections and Enforcement Services Unit of DEL utilized the trainings material to train new inspectors in the Department. The knowledge gained from the trainings and guidelines shared during the training organized by the ILO and AUDA - NEPAD was used in the development of the OHS COVID -19 directions gazetted in April 2020 and in June 2020.
The ILO also collaborated with the African Regional Labour Administration Centre (ARLAC) to host and facilitate a series of OSH courses as part of the ARLAC Basic Labour Market Academy held from 14 to 16 September 2020. The training was held virtually in a series of webinarsfocusing on OSH,including the sharing of up-to-date information to curb and mitigate the impact of COVID in the workplace.

description.narrative:
In December 2021, the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU) developed and adopted a joint Advocacy Platform with their members in vulnerable sectors of the economy to improve the protection of vulnerable workers including domestic workers. The Advocacy Platform outlines concrete actions to be undertaken to improve the rights and protection of vulnerable workers, including domestic workers.
COSATU developed and implemented a campaign, together with SADSAWU, to raise awareness amongst domestic workers about their rights under the recently amended Compensation for Occupational Injury and Disease Act (COIDA) and under Convention 189. (From October – December 2021). Under the amended COIDA domestic workers are now covered and able to claim compensation in the event that they are injured or contract diseases whilst on duty. Between August and October 2021, ILO collaborated with COSATU and its affiliate members represented by workers in vulnerable sectors of the economy to prepare for a vulnerable workers workshop held in November 2021. The workshop facilitated engagement amongst the leadership of vulnerable workers organizations on the challenges and decent work deficits faced by their members with a view towards developing an advocacy platform for the protection of the rights of vulnerable workers. The COSATU affiliate trade union members representing vulnerable workers who contributed towards the workshop preparations are notably the South Africa Taxi Drivers Workers Union (SATDWU); Trade Union for Musicians of South Africa (TUMSA); South Africa Municipal Workers Union (SAMWU) and the South Africa Domestic Workers Service and Allied Union (SADSAWU).
At the request of the South African Domestic Services and Allied Workers Union (SADSAWU), the ILO commissioned and supported the simplification of the provisions of newly amended COIDA in September 2021. The simplification of the provisions of COIDA seeks to enhance access to and understanding by domestic workers or their rights and entitlement in terms of the legislation. Once the provisions of COIDA were simplified, the ILO in November 2021, commissioned the development of communication materials that disseminated key messages coming out of the simplified COIDA amongst domestic workers across the country.
